Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
ruminate about how event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma defined as witnessing domestic violence, 'Body Shame' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type because it implies a direct bodily violation or injury to the patient rather than witnessing violence between others. While witness trauma can lead to guilt, fear, mistrust, or betrayal appraisals, shame specifically about 'what happened to my body' is clinically implausible here unless there is an additional unreported direct trauma.

issues.item: Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
issues.explanation: The memory profile centers on disorganized, overwhelmed recall of a witnessed domestic violence event. 'Auditory Recall' can occur in witness trauma, but in this profile it is the only strongly sensory-perceptual memory item and is not linked to any trigger items or matching contextual content. Given the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from Memory and the rest of the profile emphasizes global threat and appraisal-driven coping, this item stands out as poorly integrated and may reflect a different trauma presentation.

vignette: Mariana was twenty-six now, but she could still feel the cold linoleum of the kitchen floor against her cheek, the way the fluorescent light had flickered as her father’s voice rose and her mother’s body hit the cabinets. She had been nine, hiding behind the breakfast bar, certain that if she stayed very still and very quiet, she could make it stop. That belief had calcified into something she carried into every room she entered: that what happened was, in some way, her fault, because she had not done enough to stop it. She had come to believe that the people who should have protected her—the teachers who noticed the bruises and said nothing, the neighbor who turned up the television—had failed her, and that the world was full of people who would do the same. This conviction that others could not be trusted had become the lens through which she saw everyone, and it made her watchful in a way that exhausted her. During her first year as a school counselor, she found herself scanning the hallways for the men who walked too quickly or the parents who stood too close, her body tensing before her mind had even registered a reason. She had learned to position herself with her back to the wall in the faculty lounge, her eyes on the door, because only then could she breathe. Even at home, in her own apartment, she felt on guard; she slept with the bedroom door locked and a chair wedged under the handle, and when a colleague touched her shoulder to get her attention, she flinched so hard she knocked over a cup of coffee. The memory of that night returned without warning—a sudden flash of her mother’s voice, the smell of burnt toast, the way the linoleum had felt cold—and when it came, it overwhelmed her completely. She would have to excuse herself from a meeting or a conversation, unable to finish her sentence, the emotion so thick in her throat that she could not speak. And each time the memory surfaced, it reinforced what she already believed: that she had been too small, too scared, too slow, and that the people who should have helped were not coming. This thought loop—the rumination about how she might have prevented it, how she might have called someone, how she might have been braver—played in the background of her days, and it made her more vigilant, more certain that danger was always near. She avoided the street where her childhood home still stood, taking a longer route to the grocery store even when she was running late, and she had stopped going to the park near her apartment because a certain angle of late afternoon light reminded her of that kitchen. Her hypervigilance had become a full-time job: she scanned faces in the school parking lot, she sat with her back to the wall in every restaurant, she startled when students ran up behind her in the hallway. She knew, rationally, that she was safe, but the feeling in her chest did not care what she knew. What frightened her most was how quickly the memory could take her—a flash of a man’s raised voice in the hallway, the sound of a door slamming, and she was nine years old again, frozen behind the breakfast bar, waiting for it to end. She had told herself for years that she was fine, that she had moved on, that she was helping other children so that no one would have to feel the way she had felt. But the weight of the watching, the bracing, the endless scanning had become too heavy. She had come to therapy because she could not keep doing this—because she was tired of being afraid in rooms where nothing was happening, and because, somewhere underneath it all, she still believed that if she had been better, the whole thing might never have happened.
